If someone you love is looking for work, call them about something ordinary today.

Tell them what happened on your way home. Send them something that made you laugh. Ask them, “Chai pe chalein?”

They’ve probably answered “Any update?” "Kuch mila?" more times than they can count. And every time they say “Still looking,” there’s a little moment where they wish they had something better to tell you.

Maybe they’ve been meaning to call you back. Maybe they keep thinking, I’ll call when I have good news.

Call them first. Tell them you miss them. Give them an evening they can look forward to, even if their inbox is still empty.

Zomato knows what you eat at 2 AM.
Blinkit knows what you panic-buy at 2:07 AM.
And now, Deepinder Goyal wants to build an AI that knows your deepest thoughts.

Except, apparently, he doesnt want to know them either. 💀
Meet Dark.ai - Eternals latest venture into AI.
And no, its not ChatGPT with dark mode enabled.

While the AI industry is busy competing over who has the smartest model, Dark is asking a different question:What if the smartest thing an AI could do was mind its own business?

Heres whats being promised:
🔒 End-to-end encryption: Even Eternal claims it wont be able to read your conversations.🧠 Encrypted memory: Your AI remembers context across sessions, but you control that memory.
⚙️ Fine-tuned open-weight models: Running on Eternals own infrastructure.
🎯 Less people-pleasing, more truth-telling: Models designed to challenge you instead of agreeing with your questionable life decisions.

Finally, an AI that might say, This startup idea is terrible, instead of Thats a fascinating and innovative concept!

And its targeting founders, researchers, scientists, enterprises, and governments.

Basically, people whose prompts contain more trade secrets than write a professional email saying just checking in.

But heres what caught my attention from a product perspective.

Privacy isnt being positioned as a feature. Its being positioned as the product.
Thats a fascinating bet.

Because AI adoption isnt always limited by intelligence. 

Sometimes its limited by how much users trust the system with their actual thoughts.
Of course, encryption claims need technical scrutiny, and the promised model benchmarks havent been published yet.

So theres still a big gap between an impressive pitch and a proven product.
A global launch is planned for 2026.

The AI race started with Who has the smartest model? 
Maybe its next chapter is: Who can build a model smart enough to know everything you tell it, without the company knowing anything? 

Also, going from delivering midnight cravings to protecting midnight thoughts is q

Corporate loyalty is a funny concept to me.

Stay for 9 years, and your annual hikes might barely keep up with inflation.

Get laid off after 9 years, and suddenly those years of loyalty are worth 9 additional months of base pay.

I came across Microsoft's reported severance structure in India:

3 months of base pay + 1 month for every year of service.

Which got me thinking.

If companies can put a monetary value on loyalty when asking employees to leave, why does that same loyalty become so difficult to reward when they're staying?

Apparently, the secret to getting your tenure recognised is having your employment terminated.

We tell employees to think long-term, but financially incentivise them to switch every 2–3 years.

And while we're at it, why tax severance pay? Someone just lost their livelihood. That's a financial safety net, not a festive bonus.

I'm glad generous severance packages exist. But perhaps retention deserves the same creativity.

Because loyalty shouldn't be a benefit you can only encash at the exit interview.

The older I get, the more I realise that some of the most important things I've learned have had absolutely nothing to do with my career.

Nobody really prepares you for the years when you're building your future while quietly dealing with things that are breaking you in the present.

You attend meetings. Meet deadlines. Make decisions. Laugh at jokes. Talk about growth, ambition, and what's next.

And somewhere between all of that, you're also learning how to live with uncertainty, disappointment, grief, and versions of life you never planned for.

The strange thing about adulthood is that life doesn't give you time off to process life.

The world keeps moving.
And you're expected to move with it.

I've started looking at success a little differently.

There was a time when I thought success meant constantly moving forward. A better role. A bigger number. Another milestone. Something tangible to prove that I was doing well.

I still have ambitions. Quite a few, actually.

But I've realised that not everything worth achieving can be added to a résumé.

Learning to remain kind when life has made you bitter.

Learning to sit with uncertainty without desperately trying to control the outcome.

Learning that being capable doesn't mean you have to carry everything.

Learning to be proud of yourself even when nobody is watching, applauding, or acknowledging how hard something was.

And perhaps the hardest one:

Accepting that you can do everything right and still not get the outcome you hoped for.

We talk so much about resilience in the professional world.

But I think we've romanticised it a little too much.

Resilience isn't always about bouncing back stronger.

Sometimes it's about becoming softer without becoming weaker.

Sometimes it's about admitting that something hurt.

Sometimes it's about showing up for your responsibilities while giving yourself permission to be human.

I've stopped believing that every difficult experience needs to become a lesson, a motivational story, or a stepping stone to something greater.

Some experiences are simply difficult.

Some losses don't make you stronger. They just change you.

And some chapters aren't meant to be optimised. They're meant to be lived through.

Maybe growth isn't always about becoming more.

Maybe sometimes, it's about understanding what matters enough to stop chasing everything else.

Because at the end of the day, building a successful life and building a life you actually want to live are not necessarily the same thing.

And I think that's a distinction worth thinking about.

We should have 2 platforms.

Linkedin for Monday to Friday 3 pm.
Linkedout from Friday 3 pm to Monday 9 am.

LinkedIn = your professionally supervised personality.
LinkedOut = your personality after corporate parental controls expire.

LinkedIn - Mon 9 AM → Fri 3 PM
What belongs there:
“Delighted to announce…”
“Here are my 3 key learnings…”
“Failure is just feedback.”
“Leadership is not about authority. It’s about empathy.”
People pretending they enjoy networking.
“We’re hiring! 🚀”
Friday until 2:59 PM: “Another productive week!”

LinkedOut - Fri 3 PM → Mon 9 AM
Completely different ecosystem.

“After careful stakeholder alignment, we have decided: daaru.”
“My key learning this week is that it ended.”
“Let’s take this offline” → YES. PLEASE. TAKE EVERYTHING OFFLINE.

Sprint = running out of the office at 3 PM.

And the best feature of LinkedOut:
At Monday 8:59 AM:
Your LinkedOut profile will self-destruct in 60 seconds. Please remove all evidence of your actual personality.

9:00 AM:
“Good morning everyone! Hope you had a refreshing weekend. 😊”
Absolute cinema. 😭

Most people think growth is about adding more.

More skills. More titles. More achievements. More certainty.

But the deepest growth I've experienced has come from letting go.

Letting go of the need to control every outcome.
Letting go of proving my worth through constant productivity.
Letting go of the belief that every delay is a denial.

Spirituality has quietly changed the way I approach my career.

It has taught me that discipline matters more than intensity.

Presence matters more than perfection.
And intention matters more than validation.

Ironically, the less I chased external approval, the better my decisions became.

Whether you're building products, leading teams, or simply trying to become a better human, the real work isn't just learning something new.

It's unlearning what no longer serves you.

Because peace isn't the reward after success.
It's the foundation that makes meaningful success possible.

What is one belief you've unlearned that made you better at work or in life?

Signs your colleague is basically Donald Trump (corporate edition):

1. Every meeting starts with:
“This is going to be the greatest project ever.”
Ends with: “We’ll figure out the details later.”

2. New plan every 24 hours.
Yesterday: “Focus on stability.”
Today: “Let’s pivot. Disruption is key.”
Tomorrow: “Why did we lose stability?”

3. Loves announcements more than execution.
Big vision slides ✔️
Actual roadmap ❌

4. Takes credit faster than your app loads.
“Team effort” in private.
“My leadership” in front of leadership.

5. Communication style = confidence over clarity.
You leave meetings with:
energy 📈
understanding 📉

6. If something fails…
“It was already broken when I got it.”
If something works…
“I personally ensured this success.”

7. Uses big words to hide small plans.
“Revolutionizing the ecosystem”
= changing button color.

8. Feedback?
Only one direction.
Top → down.
Bottom → career risk.

9. Deadlines are… flexible.
Except when it’s your task.
Then it’s “why is this delayed?”

10. Strategy = vibes.
Roadmap = opinions.
Execution = your problem.

But honestly…
the biggest sign?

You spend more time understanding your manager’s statements
than understanding your actual product.

Everyone thinks they’re getting rejected because of competition.

But here’s the uncomfortable truth:
Most resumes don’t even reach a human.
They die… in silence… inside an ATS.

Not because you’re not skilled.
Not because you’re not worthy.

But because your resume is speaking a language the system doesn’t understand.

Imagine this:
You spent 4 years building skills
2 years gaining experience
Countless nights preparing
And your resume gets rejected in 6 seconds
By a machine.

No feedback.
No explanation.

Just… gone.

Here’s what most people get wrong:
They treat a resume like a document.
It’s not.
It’s a PRODUCT.

And like every product:
If it’s not built for the user (ATS + recruiter), it won’t convert.

Let me show you what actually works:

Keywords are not optional
If the job says “stakeholder management” and your resume says “handled teams” → you’re invisible

Fancy ≠ effective
Design-heavy resumes often break ATS parsing
Simple > stylish

Impact beats responsibility
“Responsible for dashboards” ❌
“Increased reporting efficiency by 32% using automated dashboards” ✅

Structure matters more than content
If your resume is not scannable in 5 - 7 seconds, it’s already rejected

One resume ≠ all jobs
If you’re mass applying with one resume, you’re mass getting rejected

And the biggest mistake?
People think:
“Resume toh bana hi liya hai, ab bas apply karna hai”
No.

Resume is not step 1.
Resume is the conversion engine.

I’ve seen insanely talented people struggle
Just because their resume couldn’t tell their story right.
And average profiles…
Getting shortlisted.
